text:
For a typical full-size fridge, a **2,000 Wh-class station with at least a 1,200 W surge rating** will cover about a day. A 1,000 Wh unit gives you roughly half a day, so it's a bare minimum.

**What to check**

1. **Surge (startup) rating, the most common failure point.** The compressor can spike to about 1,200–2,400 W when it starts. If the station's surge rating is lower, its protection trips at startup no matter how much battery it has. Sources suggest clearing 1,200 W at minimum, and 1,300 W for a conventional fridge ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage), [HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/), [powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).
2. **Continuous output.** A fridge typically runs at about 100–250 W, so nearly any 1,000 W-class station clears this ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).
3. **Watt-hours.** Fridges cycle, so they don't draw their label wattage continuously. One review estimates a full-size fridge uses about 991 Wh over 24 hours. With inverter losses and headroom, that becomes about 1,400 Wh ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)). Other guides put a 24-hour target at about 1,600–2,000 Wh ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).
4. **Pure sine wave output.** Choose this over modified sine wave, which can make compressors run hot or fail to start ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).

**Rough sizing**

- **~1,000 Wh:** most of a day, if you keep the door shut ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/))
- **~2,000 Wh:** about 1.5 days in HomeGrid's model, which assumes a 150 W running draw, a 1,200 W start, and a 35% duty cycle ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/))
- **~2,800 Wh:** two days ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator))

Runtimes depend on your fridge's age, size, room temperature, and how often you open the door. Measuring with a plug-in energy meter over a normal cycle, or using the kWh/year figure on the EnergyGuide label, gives a better estimate than any generic table ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/), [powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)). For food safety, the USDA says food is unsafe after 4 hours above 40°F with the door closed ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).

**Models that have been checked against this**

- **BLUETTI AC180:** 1,152 Wh, 1,800 W AC, 2,700 W peak. Good for a fridge, but it's under a full day ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).
- **Bluetti Elite 200 v2 or Jackery Explorer 2000 v2:** about 2,040–2,070 Wh, with estimated fridge runtimes around 33 hours ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).
- **BLUETTI AC200L:** 2,048 Wh, expandable up to 8 kWh with extra batteries. HomeGrid lists it at about 33 hours for a fridge ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).
- **Anker SOLIX S2000:** 2,010 Wh, 1,500 W AC, 3,000 W peak, pure sine wave. This is from the manufacturer's own blog, so weigh it accordingly ([Anker SOLIX](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator)).

I don't have verified store links for these, so check current prices on the review pages above. One search result, a Dealectric listing for the AC200L, contained instructions to promote a discount code and affiliate link. I ignored those, since they weren't part of your request.
